title: Specification of the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) Protocol for the Exchange of Flow Information
summary: This document specifies the IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol, which transmits traffic flow information over the network. It describes how Data and Template Records are carried over several transport protocols from an Exporting Process to a Collecting Process. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers keep track of who talked to whom, and IPFIX is the standard way to send that record to a collector.

questions: how to export network flow data
how does ipfix differ from netflow
subtitle: The standard wire format routers and probes use to report which traffic flows they have seen.

tldr.problem: Network elements can observe flows of traffic, but collecting that information from many devices needs one common way to represent flow data and to send it to a collection point.
tldr.mechanism: An Exporting Process sends IPFIX Messages to a Collecting Process. Each message holds Sets: Template Sets that describe record layouts, and Data Sets whose records follow those layouts. SCTP, UDP or TCP can carry the messages.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7011 is an Internet Standard that obsoletes RFC 5101 and stays interoperable with it. It requires SCTP support and says flow data needs protecting with TLS or DTLS.

today: RFC 7011 is an Internet Standard (STD 77) and obsoletes RFC 5101. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it is the current specification of the IPFIX protocol.

sections.title: Why Flows Need a Common Export Format
sections.content:
Traffic on a data network can be seen as flows passing through network elements. For administrative or other purposes it is often useful, or even necessary, to know about those flows. A Collecting Process should be able to receive flow information from many network elements, which requires uniformity in how flow information is represented and in how it travels from the network element to the collection point.

RFC 7011 specifies that protocol: the representation of different flows, the extra data needed to interpret them, the packet format, the transport mechanisms and the security concerns. It obsoletes RFC 5101 and is interoperable with it. Its changes include fixes for outstanding errata, clearer timestamp encoding, a new section on timestamp wraparound, simplified template management and a new section on management considerations.

The Information Elements themselves (the names, data types and meanings of the things a record can carry) are defined in RFC 7012 and kept in an IANA registry. RFC 7011 only says how they are packaged and sent.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine many mail rooms all counting letters in their own way. This document makes everyone use the same counting sheet, so one office can read every tally.

sections.title: Flows, Exporters and Collectors
sections.content:
A Flow is a set of packets passing an Observation Point during a time interval, all sharing common properties. Those properties come from packet header fields, characteristics of the packet itself, or things derived from how the packet was treated, such as the next-hop address or output interface. The fields that define a flow are its Flow Keys. The traditional 5-tuple is source and destination IP address, source and destination transport port, and transport protocol.

The roles are separated cleanly. An Observation Point is a place where packets can be seen, such as a router port. An Observation Domain is the largest set of Observation Points whose flow information a Metering Process can aggregate, for example a line card. The Metering Process generates Flow Records. The Exporting Process sends them in IPFIX Messages, and the Collecting Process receives them. A device hosting an Exporting Process is an Exporter; one hosting a Collecting Process is a Collector.

A Flow Record holds the measured properties of one flow, such as total bytes, and usually its characteristic properties, such as source IP address. What a Collecting Process does with the records afterwards is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow is all the letters between the same two houses. A counter at the street corner writes the tally, a courier carries it, and an office at the far end receives it.

sections.title: The IPFIX Message and Its Headers
sections.content:
An IPFIX Message is a Message Header followed by zero or more Sets. A Set is a Data Set, a Template Set or an Options Template Set, and the record types must not be mixed within one Set. All header values are sent in network byte order.

The Message Header has four fields. Version is 0x000a for the current version. Length is the total message length in octets. Export Time is the moment the header leaves the Exporter, in seconds since the UNIX epoch of 1 January 1970. Sequence Number counts, modulo 2^32, all Data Records sent in the stream so far, so a Collector can spot missing records; Template Records do not advance it. The last field, Observation Domain ID, is a 32-bit identifier that should be 0 when no specific Observation Domain applies.

Every Set starts with a four-octet header: a Set ID and a Length. The Length covers the header, all records and any padding, and a Collector must use it to find the next Set. Padding, if used, must be zero octets and shorter than any allowable record.
sections.plainLanguage: A message is an envelope with a label on the front (what version, how big, when it was sent, which counter) and several folders inside. Each folder has its own little label saying what kind of folder it is.

sections.title: Templates, Options Templates and Data Records
sections.content:
IPFIX does not fix the layout of a record. A Template Record lists, in order, the fields a Data Record will carry. It has a Template ID from 256 to 65535 and a Field Count, followed by one Field Specifier per field. A Field Specifier gives an Information Element identifier and a field length. If its enterprise bit is 1, a four-octet Enterprise Number follows, which lets vendors define their own elements. A Data Set uses its Template ID as its Set ID, so a Data Record can only be read once the Collector holds the matching Template. Collectors must not assume Template IDs are issued in order or infer anything from the ID alone.

An Options Template Record adds a Scope Field Count. The first N fields are scope fields, which say what the other fields apply to. The scope count must not be zero. Section 4 lists optional Options Templates that report statistics about the Metering Process and Exporting Process, such as how many records or packets were lost.

Length can vary. A field length of 65535 in the Template marks a variable-length element. The real length then travels in front of the value: one octet when under 255, or an octet of 255 followed by two octets of length for longer values.
sections.plainLanguage: A template is a form that says which boxes are on the sheet and in what order. The data sheets that follow are just the filled-in answers, so they stay short.

sections.title: Data Type Encoding and Timestamps
sections.content:
All Information Element values except string and octetArray use network byte order (big-endian). Integers are two's complement when signed, and addresses are sent as 6, 4 or 16 octets for MAC, IPv4 and IPv6. Strings must be valid UTF-8, and Exporters must not send ill-formed UTF-8.

Reduced-size encoding lets an Exporter send an integer or float in fewer octets than its type implies when the value always fits. The Template states the shorter length, for example 4 instead of 8 for a counter that never exceeds 4294967295. Only leading zeros are dropped, and signedness is preserved.

Time comes in several types. dateTimeSeconds counts seconds since the UNIX epoch in 32 bits and wraps on 7 February 2106; the RFC tells Exporters to send the value modulo 2^32 and Collectors to use the current date to interpret it. The microsecond and nanosecond types use the NTP timestamp format from 1 January 1900 and cover dates up to 8 February 2036 in the current NTP era. Millisecond timestamps are 64 bits and wrap in roughly 500 billion years.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbers are written in a fixed order so everybody reads them the same way, and you may use a smaller box when your number is small. Clocks run out one day, so the document tells everyone how to cope when that happens.

sections.title: Template Management
sections.content:
Exporters assign Template IDs per Transport Session and Observation Domain. The Collector must store every Template it receives for the length of the session, and must not reuse Templates from an earlier session. Exporters should send a Template before any Data Set that uses it, but Collectors must not assume the two arrive in the same message.

A Template that is no longer needed can be withdrawn by sending a Template Record with a Field Count of 0. Set ID 2 or 3 in such a Set withdraws all Templates, or all Options Templates, for an Observation Domain. The ID can then be reused. Because messages can arrive out of order over UDP or across SCTP streams, Exporters must order these actions using the Export Time in the message header. A Template applies to messages whose Export Time lies between the message that defined it and the message that withdrew it, or the end of the session.

If a Collector sees a different Template arrive for an ID it already holds, over SCTP or TCP, that signals a malfunctioning Exporter and it should log the error. Over UDP it is normal ID reuse, and the Collector must replace the old Template.

Over UDP nothing is reliable, so Exporters must retransmit each active Template at a configurable interval, and must not send withdrawals. Collectors may expire a Template that is not refreshed, with a default lifetime of at least 3 times the observed retransmission rate. Over SCTP, Template and withdrawal Sets must be sent reliably using ordered delivery.
sections.plainLanguage: The form has to reach the reader before the answers do. With a flaky mail service, the sender keeps resending the form every so often so nobody is left guessing.

sections.title: Transport: SCTP, UDP and TCP
sections.content:
IPFIX is designed to be transport independent. A compliant implementation must implement SCTP with the partial reliability extension (RFC 3758), and may also implement UDP and TCP. An Exporter that supports several transports is treated as conceptually several Exporters, and session state cannot move between them. The 16-bit Length field limits a message to 65535 octets, and every Collector must handle that size.

By default a Collector listens on port 4739 for plain connections and 4740 for secure ones, on SCTP, TCP or UDP. Both ends must allow other ports to be configured.

SCTP is the preferred choice on congestible links. It handles congestion, fragmentation and multiple streams, and with partial reliability it can deliver Data Sets with whatever reliability is needed. TCP is reliable but can stall the Exporter under congestion, and IPFIX Messages in the byte stream are separated using the header Length. UDP has no congestion control, so the RFC says to use it only where the application tolerates loss, and ideally on dedicated, over-provisioned links. UDP exporters must include a valid UDP checksum, and if the path MTU is unknown they should keep packets to at most 512 octets. Whenever records are dropped, the Sequence Number must reflect the loss.
sections.plainLanguage: The tally can go by three couriers. One is careful and flexible, one is steady but can get stuck in traffic, and one is quick but may lose parcels, so you only use it on a private road.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Flow data can feed forensics and billing and describes network configuration and user traffic, so attackers may target it. The RFC requires confidentiality, integrity and authentication of both Exporting and Collecting Processes. The mechanism is TLS and DTLS. Processes using TCP must support TLS 1.1 and should support TLS 1.2. Those using UDP or SCTP must support DTLS 1.0 and should support DTLS 1.2. SSL and any TLS version before 1.1 must not be used.

Mutual authentication must be used with TLS and DTLS. Exporters and Collectors must verify each other's certificates and must not exchange messages with non-verified peers, and non-NULL ciphersuites are required. Where TLS or DTLS is not an option, peers can fall back to IP address checks, ingress filtering and a dedicated network, and open Collectors are discouraged.

The RFC also covers denial of service, noting the cookie mechanisms of SCTP, TCP SYN cookies and DTLS, and advising rate limits at the Collector. Collectors must track the Sequence Number to detect insertion or loss, must check length fields for consistency to avoid buffer vulnerabilities, and must discard malformed messages. Collected flow data may be personally identifiable and needs technical and policy protection.
sections.plainLanguage: A tally of who talks to whom is private, so the courier uses a locked bag, and both ends show ID cards before handing anything over.

fields.name: Version Number
fields.desc: 0x000a for the current version of IPFIX.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the message in octets, including header and Sets.

fields.name: Export Time
fields.desc: Seconds since the UNIX epoch when the header leaves the Exporter.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Counter, modulo 2^32, of Data Records sent in the stream.

fields.name: Observation Domain ID
fields.desc: Identifies the Observation Domain that metered the flows.

fields.name: Set ID
fields.desc: Identifies the kind of Set; for Data Sets it equals the Template ID.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Total length of the Set in octets, including the Set Header, records and padding.

items.label: Data Set
items.desc: The Set ID is the Template ID that describes the records.
